questions.explanation_text: Since $2^{x}$ can be written as $2^{x}=e^{xlog2}$ the integrand becomes $e^{-xlog2} \cdot 2^{x}=e^{-xlog2} \cdot e^{xlog2}$ Using $e^{a} \cdot e^{b}=e^{a+b}$ , $e^{-xlog2+xlog2}=e^{0}=1$ So the integral is $\int 1dx=x+C$ So the correct option is $x+C$ Option B.

questions.question_text: If ' $n$ ' is a natural number, then $\int \frac{sin^{n}x}{cos^{n+2}x}dx=$
questions.question_html: If ' $n$ ' is a natural number, then $\int \frac{sin^{n}x}{cos^{n+2}x}dx=$
questions.explanation_text: Given, $\int \frac{sin^{n}x}{cos^{n+2}x}dx$ We can rewrite the integrand by separating powers of $cosx$ : $\frac{sin^{n}x}{cos^{n+2}x}=\frac{sin^{n}x}{cos^{n}x} \cdot \frac{1}{cos^{2}x}$ Now, $\frac{sinx}{cosx}=tanx$ and $\frac{1}{cos^{2}x}=sec^{2}x$ So, $\frac{sin^{n}x}{cos^{n+2}x}=tan^{n}xsec^{2}x$ Hence, $\int \frac{sin^{n}x}{cos^{n+2}x}dx=\int tan^{n}xsec^{2}xdx$ Put $t=tanx$ Then, $dt=sec^{2}xdx$ So the integral becomes $\int t^{n}dt=\frac{t^{n+1}}{n+1}+C$ Putting back $t=tanx$ , $\int \frac{sin^{n}x}{cos^{n+2}x}dx=\frac{tan^{n+1}x}{n+1}+C$ So the correct option is $\text{Option D}\frac{tan^{n+1}x}{n+1}+C$
questions.explanation_html:
Given,

$\int \frac{sin^{n}x}{cos^{n+2}x}dx$

We can rewrite the integrand by separating powers of $cosx$ :

$\frac{sin^{n}x}{cos^{n+2}x}=\frac{sin^{n}x}{cos^{n}x} \cdot \frac{1}{cos^{2}x}$

Now,

$\frac{sinx}{cosx}=tanx$

and

$\frac{1}{cos^{2}x}=sec^{2}x$

So,

$\frac{sin^{n}x}{cos^{n+2}x}=tan^{n}xsec^{2}x$

Hence,

$\int \frac{sin^{n}x}{cos^{n+2}x}dx=\int tan^{n}xsec^{2}xdx$

Put

$t=tanx$

Then,

$dt=sec^{2}xdx$

So the integral becomes

$\int t^{n}dt=\frac{t^{n+1}}{n+1}+C$

Putting back $t=tanx$ ,

$\int \frac{sin^{n}x}{cos^{n+2}x}dx=\frac{tan^{n+1}x}{n+1}+C$

So the correct option is

$\text{Option D}\frac{tan^{n+1}x}{n+1}+C$

questions.explanation_text: Let $I=\int \frac{1}{1+3sin^{2}x+8cos^{2}x}dx$ Dividing the numerator and denominator by $cos^{2}x$ , we get $\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow I=\int \frac{sec^{2}x}{sec^{2}x+3tan^{2}x+8}dx \\ & \Rightarrow I=\int \frac{sec^{2}x}{1+tan^{2}x+3tan^{2}x+8}dx \\ & \Rightarrow I=\int \frac{sec^{2}x}{4tan^{2}x+9}dx \end{aligned}$ Putting, $tanx=t \Rightarrow sec^{2}xdx=dt$ , we get $\begin{aligned} & I=\int \frac{dt}{4t^{2}+9}=\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{dt}{t^{2}+(\frac{3}{2})^{2}}+C \\ I & =\frac{1}{4} \times \frac{1}{3/2}tan^{-1}(\frac{t}{3/2})+C \\ \Rightarrow I & =\frac{1}{6}tan^{-1}(\frac{2t}{3})+C=\frac{1}{6}tan^{-1}(\frac{2tanx}{3})+C \end{aligned}$

questions.question_html: If $\int \frac{dx}{(x+2)(x^{2}+1)}=alog|1+x^{2}|+btan^{-1}x+\frac{1}{5}log|x+2|+c,$ then
questions.explanation_text: Given, $\int \frac{dx}{(x+2)(x^{2}+1)}=alog|1+x^{2}|+btan^{-1}x+\frac{1}{5}log|x+2|+c$ .... (i) $\begin{aligned} & \text{Let}\frac{1}{(x+2)(x^{2}+1)}=\frac{A}{(x+2)}+\frac{Bx+C}{(x^{2}+1)} \\ & \therefore 1=A(x^{2}+1)+(x+2)(Bx+C) \\ & 1=Ax^{2}+A+Bx^{2}+Cx+2Bx+2C \\ & 1=(A+B)x^{2}+x(2B+C)+A+2C \end{aligned}$ Here, $A+B=0$ , $2B+C=0\text{and}A+2C=1$ On solving them, we get $A=\frac{1}{5},B=\frac{-1}{5}\text{and}C=\frac{2}{5}$ Therefore, $\int \frac{dx}{(x+2)(x^{2}+1)}$ $\begin{aligned} & =\int (\frac{1}{5(x+2)}+\frac{\frac{-1}{5}x+\frac{2}{5}}{x^{2}+1}) \\ & =\frac{1}{5}\int \frac{1}{(x+2)}dx-\frac{1}{5}\int \frac{x}{x^{2}+1}dx+\frac{2}{5}\int \frac{dx}{1+x^{2}} \\ & =\frac{1}{5}log|x+2|-\frac{1}{10}log|1+x^{2}|+\frac{2}{5}tan^{-1}x+c \\ & =-\frac{1}{10}log(1+x^{2})+\frac{2}{5}tan^{-1}x+\frac{1}{5}log|x+2|+c\text{.... (ii)} \end{aligned}$ On comparing Eqs. (i) and (ii), we get $a=\frac{-1}{10}\text{and}b=\frac{2}{5}$
questions.explanation_html:
Given,

$\int \frac{dx}{(x+2)(x^{2}+1)}=alog|1+x^{2}|+btan^{-1}x+\frac{1}{5}log|x+2|+c$ .... (i)

$\begin{aligned} & \text{Let}\frac{1}{(x+2)(x^{2}+1)}=\frac{A}{(x+2)}+\frac{Bx+C}{(x^{2}+1)} \\ & \therefore 1=A(x^{2}+1)+(x+2)(Bx+C) \\ & 1=Ax^{2}+A+Bx^{2}+Cx+2Bx+2C \\ & 1=(A+B)x^{2}+x(2B+C)+A+2C \end{aligned}$

Here, $A+B=0$ ,

$2B+C=0\text{and}A+2C=1$

On solving them, we get

$A=\frac{1}{5},B=\frac{-1}{5}\text{and}C=\frac{2}{5}$

Therefore, $\int \frac{dx}{(x+2)(x^{2}+1)}$

$\begin{aligned} & =\int (\frac{1}{5(x+2)}+\frac{\frac{-1}{5}x+\frac{2}{5}}{x^{2}+1}) \\ & =\frac{1}{5}\int \frac{1}{(x+2)}dx-\frac{1}{5}\int \frac{x}{x^{2}+1}dx+\frac{2}{5}\int \frac{dx}{1+x^{2}} \\ & =\frac{1}{5}log|x+2|-\frac{1}{10}log|1+x^{2}|+\frac{2}{5}tan^{-1}x+c \\ & =-\frac{1}{10}log(1+x^{2})+\frac{2}{5}tan^{-1}x+\frac{1}{5}log|x+2|+c\text{.... (ii)} \end{aligned}$

On comparing Eqs. (i) and (ii), we get

$a=\frac{-1}{10}\text{and}b=\frac{2}{5}$

questions.explanation_text: $\begin{aligned} \text{Let}I & =\int \frac{xe^{x}dx}{(1+x)^{2}} \\ & =\int \frac{e^{x}(x+1-1)}{(1+x)^{2}}dx \\ & =\int e^{x}[\frac{1}{1+x}+(\frac{-1}{(1+x)^{2}})]dx \end{aligned}$ Let $\frac{1}{1+x}=f(x)$ $\therefore f^{'}(x)=-\frac{1}{(1+x)^{2}}$ Using the formula, $\int e^{x}[f(x)+f^{'}(x)]dx$ $\begin{aligned} & =e^{x}f(x)+C \\ \Rightarrow I & =e^{x}(\frac{1}{1+x})+C=\frac{e^{x}}{1+x}+C \end{aligned}$

questions.explanation_text: To solve the integral $\int e^{sinx} \cdot (\frac{sinx+1}{secx})dx$ , let's start with the given function: $I=\int e^{sinx} \cdot (\frac{sinx+1}{secx})dx$ This can be rewritten as: $I=\int e^{sinx} \cdot (sinx+1)cosxdx$ To simplify, we perform a substitution. Let $sinx=t$ . Then, the derivative is: $cosxdx=dt$ Substituting these into the integral, we get: $I=\int e^{t}(t+1)dt$ We recognize that this integral can be solved using the formula: $\int e^{x}{f(x)+f^{'}(x)}dx=e^{x}f(x)+C$ Applying this formula with $f(x)=t$ and $f^{'}(x)=1$ , we have: $I=te^{t}+C$ Substituting back $t=sinx$ , we arrive at the solution: $I=sinx \cdot e^{sinx}+C$

questions.explanation_text: Let's evaluate the integral: $I=\int \frac{1}{1+e^{x}}dx$ First, rewrite the integrand: $I=\int \frac{e^{-x}}{e^{-x}+1}dx$ Now, use the substitution method. Let: $u=e^{-x}+1$ Differentiating both sides with respect to $x$ , we get: $\frac{du}{dx}=-e^{-x} \Rightarrow -e^{-x}dx=du$ Substituting, the integral becomes: $I=-\int \frac{1}{u}du$ This integral simplifies to: $I=-log|u|+C$ Substitute back $u=e^{-x}+1$ : $I=-log(e^{-x}+1)+C$ Using the properties of logarithms: $I=log(\frac{1}{e^{-x}+1})+C$ Rewriting $\frac{1}{e^{-x}+1}$ in terms of $e^{x}$ : $I=log(\frac{e^{x}}{e^{x}+1})+C$ So, the final answer is: $I=log(\frac{e^{x}}{e^{x}+1})+C$

$I=\int \frac{e^{-x}}{e^{-x}+1}dx$

Now, use the substitution method. Let:

$u=e^{-x}+1$

Differentiating both sides with respect to $x$ , we get:

$\frac{du}{dx}=-e^{-x} \Rightarrow -e^{-x}dx=du$

Substituting, the integral becomes:

So, the final answer is:

$I=log(\frac{e^{x}}{e^{x}+1})+C$

questions.question_html: $\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{3-6x-9x^{2}}}dx$ is equal to
questions.explanation_text: We need to evaluate the integral: $I=\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{3-6x-9x^{2}}}dx$ First, let's rewrite the expression under the square root: $I=\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{3-(9x^{2}+6x+1)+1}}dx$ Notice that $9x^{2}+6x+1$ can be rewritten to form a perfect square. We have: $9x^{2}+6x+1=(3x+1)^{2}$ Therefore, the integral becomes: $I=\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{(2)^{2}-(3x+1)^{2}}}dx$ Next, let's perform a substitution. Let: $3x+1=t$ Then the differential becomes: $d(3x+1)=dt⟹3dx=dt \Rightarrow dx=\frac{1}{3}dt$ Substituting these into the integral, we get: $I=\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{(2)^{2}-t^{2}}}dt$ The integral $\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{a^{2}-t^{2}}}dt$ is recognized as the inverse sine function: $\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{a^{2}-t^{2}}}dt=sin^{-1}(\frac{t}{a})+C$ Applying this formula with $a=2$ , we have: $I=\frac{1}{3}sin^{-1}(\frac{t}{2})+C$ Substitute back $t=3x+1$ : $I=\frac{1}{3}sin^{-1}(\frac{3x+1}{2})+C$
questions.explanation_html:
We need to evaluate the integral:

$I=\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{3-6x-9x^{2}}}dx$

First, let's rewrite the expression under the square root:

$I=\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{3-(9x^{2}+6x+1)+1}}dx$

Notice that $9x^{2}+6x+1$ can be rewritten to form a perfect square. We have:

$9x^{2}+6x+1=(3x+1)^{2}$

Therefore, the integral becomes:

$I=\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{(2)^{2}-(3x+1)^{2}}}dx$

Next, let's perform a substitution. Let:

$3x+1=t$

Then the differential becomes:

$d(3x+1)=dt⟹3dx=dt \Rightarrow dx=\frac{1}{3}dt$

Substituting these into the integral, we get:

$I=\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{(2)^{2}-t^{2}}}dt$

The integral $\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{a^{2}-t^{2}}}dt$ is recognized as the inverse sine function:

$\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{a^{2}-t^{2}}}dt=sin^{-1}(\frac{t}{a})+C$

Applying this formula with $a=2$ , we have:

$I=\frac{1}{3}sin^{-1}(\frac{t}{2})+C$

Substitute back $t=3x+1$ :

$I=\frac{1}{3}sin^{-1}(\frac{3x+1}{2})+C$
